utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Good afternoon, Mr. Mujkic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic, are you ready to begin your cross-examination? Yes, let's start.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Excellencies. Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mujkic.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, I will try to put, as simple as possible, my questions. And whenever it suits you, you can answer with a yes or a no, because we don't have too much time. Is it correct that in March 1996, you gave a statement to the AID in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I provided a statement at the police in the Novi Grad municipality. I don't know whether that was the AID or someone else. I didn't ask. I wasn't really interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this was four years after the events; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in the statement, did you describe in detail the events from May and June, and then from August, that pertained to the Rajlovac Barracks?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't mention the Rajlovac Barracks because I didn't know the purpose of their being there. So I really didn't want to give an incomplete statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's refresh your memory a little bit. So let's look at 65 ter 22188 in the e-court, please. Can we look at the first page, please, so Mr. Mujkic can identify the document. And then we will go to the seventh page in the Serbian the ninth page in the English. This is the e-court pages or pages 18 -- pages 19 and 22 in the document, itself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this your statement from -- actually, this is a Rule 92 bis bundle which contains the statement. Can we look at page 19 in the e-court from this bundle of documents, and that will be page 22 in the English. Page 22 in the English in the e-court. We also need to look at the page in the Serbian. In the English, it's in the middle somewhere, where it says "Apostolski" and "Karadzic." My name is there. Can we have the Serbian version. Actually, would you please leave the English version on the screen, even though Mr. Mujkic would need to look at the Serbian version. And can we look at the English on the other half of the screen now, please. It's 22 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at the bottom third of the page, where we see that it says: "In the morning, Mile Tintor came in, son of Mirko ..." And so on and so forth. Can you look at that. Here, it's somewhere in the middle. It's on the bottom half of the page: "In the morning ..." Yes, this is in the English. Can you please look at this paragraph: "I used to see him in Ahatovici, how he was, and so that he was looting the stolen property." Is this a description of the visit of these people to you while you were captured, while you were a prisoner, a prisoner at the Rajlovac Barracks?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, in June 1997, you gave a statement to the Prosecutor's Office of this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at your description of this event in the statement. Can we look at 65 ter 22188. I think it's the same document, but we just need to look at the 10th page in the Serbian and the 11th in the English in the e-court. Same document, page 10 in the Serbian, page 11 in the English. Page 10 in the Serbian, page 11 in the English. The following page in the English, please. This is the sixth paragraph from the top or the third from the bottom: "While I was ..." No, no, this is in the hospital. We're talking about Rajlovac: "While I was in Rajlovac on the 7th of August, 1992, I was visited by Goran Lemez and Major Vlasto Apostolski. I asked Goran for a cigarette. The major told me, 'His name is not Goran; he is a vojvoda, a duke.' "Goran had a lot of paper regarding other prisoners."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you describe Huso Gacanovic and Asim Novalija were brought to Rajlovac, and so on and so forth. Is this a correct description? Did you provide that statement?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you say that he was a member of the SDS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To this vojvoda.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Lemez? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the SDS did not have any titles, it didn't give anybody a title, nor did it tolerate anybody having any kinds of titles?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know exactly who said what. I didn't know about the titles, but this is how they introduced themselves. Vlasto Apostolski would always say, This person is a "vojvoda." For another person, he said he was a "nadvojvoda," an archduke. I don't know how they issued these titles or what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, we will find out later. In this passage, you describe that these two persons also visited you in the Rajlovac Barracks on the 7th of August 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this was during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you gave another statement on the 24th of March, 1998, where, for the third time, you described your stay at the Rajlovac Barracks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the dates anymore, what statement I provided, when. What does it say in the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, let's refresh your memory. Can we look at 1D3269, please. 1D3269, 3269.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Allow me to read this for you. Everybody can follow. We can look at the first paragraph, the first two or three sentences: "After my wounding and capture on the 6th of April, 1992, I know that: that on the 6th of August, 1992, in the late evening hours, Goran Lemez came to my cell at the Rajlovac Barracks, together with the Rajlovac Brigade police commander, Vlasto Apostolovski, and asked me to give a statement." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the second person who entered my cell. The first one was Mile Stojanovic, but Goran came to me on the 7th as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Later, we will tender this when we finish with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After this statement to the OTP, you gave an additional statement on the 8th of April, 2009; is that -- 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, because I was at the Tribunal in Nedzarici, I provided a statement there on two occasions. In 2004, I gave a statement. I really cannot remember the dates, when I gave which statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. This is your statement that we're looking at on the screen right now; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that it's signed with my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is page 1. Did you give a statement like this?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult to read. I cannot read it, and there is no signature.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We received this from the OTP as your statement. Can we now look at 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we show him the next page, the next page and on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can, but we're just wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, in B/C/S. Just a second. No, this is not the -- second page. That's the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And was it your signature you saw at page 4? Show him the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did see the signature here. I didn't see my signature in the earlier pages, and the place for the signature was blank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is this your statement that was retyped, and you actually signed your handwritten; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D3268, please. This is an additional supplemental statement that you gave on the 28th of April, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at this second paragraph. Can we look at that: "Regarding the incident that took place on the 6th of August, 1992, when I was wounded and captured by the members of the Serb military formations, I now do remember chronologically that I was transported by TAM to the Rajlovac Barracks in the evening hours and put in an improvised cell. Stojanovic, Mile, came to take my personal details later on. Lemez, Goran, and Apostolovski, Vlasto, a Macedonian, an active serviceman who was employed in the former JNA barracks in Rajlovac before the war as a 'plavac,' member of the air force in the rank of captain first class ..." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We don't need to continue reading. Everyone can read that. Can we read the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters, kindly, would like to look at the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The original is in e-court. The interpreters should be able to see them. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic. Could you repeat the last part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the following paragraph. I haven't read the first one. It's the second evening. In the English, we would need to look at the next page: "On the next evening, Mile Tintor, who was in civilian clothing, and Lasta Apostolovski, came to the cell. After they entered the cell, and when they saw me, Tintor addressed Apostolovski, 'What are you doing with the wounded people, Major?' Then Apostolovski started to exonerate himself and shrugged his shoulders. After that, Tintor again addressed Apostolovski, 'Major, if anyone touches Ramiz from now on, you will see who Mile Tintor is.' After that, nobody beat me, but they kept on taking Gacanovic, Huso ...," and so on and so forth, "out." So these two visits that you described here, and as say you were visited by Lemez and Apostolovski, before that Mile Stojanovic, and after that Tintor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mile came in the afternoon, so I don't know why it says there that it was in the evening. It was still light. In August, the days are long. It's true that he did say that to Vlasto, and it's true that nobody ever touched me after that, but they did beat these other two men, Asim Novalija and the other guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So a year after this supplemental statement, year and a half after the supplemental statement, again you meet with the OTP of this Tribunal, and for the fifth time you give an explanation in relation to your statement from 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really cannot be sure of the dates again. I should have kept a diary in order to keep track of everything. I cannot remember all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, we will call up these documents. You have the right to refresh your memory. Can we now look at 65 ter 22188 now, please, page 4 in e-court, and page 5 in English. Let's look at paragraph 3 from the bottom in both versions. It says: "Page 5, paragraph 5, lines 1 and 2: It should be clarified that when I was wounded and taken prisoner in Ilijas municipality, I was driven to the Rajlovac Barracks in a TAM truck which belonged to the Butile Barracks before the war and which had been at that time before the war driven by Nikola Stanisic. On that day when I was driven into the Rajlovac Barracks, the truck was driven by Slavisa Koprivica." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, you were summoned to come and testify in the Momcilo Krajisnik case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was in 2004, 12 years after the event and 5 years after you gave these statements and provided the addendum to the statements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's approximately the time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this testimony of yours is preceded by five statements, one addendum to the statement, and your evidence given in the Krajisnik case. You said that on the 7th of August, you were visited at Rajlovac Barracks by the brother of Momcilo Krajisnik as well, whom you had never seen before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you like to see this to refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need. I lived through it, and everything is in my head. No need for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at your amalgamated witness statement, which is 65 ter 90219. The question was mistranslated, although I'm speaking more slowly. Therefore, my proposition is that: After five statements and addendums and twelve years after the event, for the first time in the trial against Momcilo Krajisnik, you mentioned that his brother came to visit you while you were in the cell; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at your amalgamated statement, page 12, paragraph 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first visit by Mile Stojanovic, the second visit by Goran and Apostolski, the third visit Tintor and Apostolski; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The third visit was paid by these three gentlemen, Mr. Poplasen and Mirko, and the third person was in uniform. He didn't say a word. I didn't know him, and he never addressed me. Of course, it was Vlasto Apostolski who brought him in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you just mention the name of Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to read it to you, paragraph 59, and it will be translated to you: [In English] "On the 7th of August, 1992, I received the third visit to my cell that night. Major Vlasto Apostolski came in. He was the commander of the military police of the Rajlovac Brigade, and three men came in after him. I knew Apostolski from before. He was an active captain. He introduced them and said of one, This is 'nadvojvoda.' This man who was introduced as "nadvojvoda" was of middle build, perhaps a bit skinny, and with a beard. This man was in civilian clothes. I recalled him immediately as Nikola Poplasen because I used to see him from the TV. He also had specific accent that wasn't from Sarajevo. One of the other men was Mirko Krajisnik, who I recognised. I didn't recognise the third man, and he didn't introduce him either. Krajisnik asked me to tell them where Hasan Mujkic was hiding and Husein Mujkic, two brothers. Hasan Mujkic was the head of the Ahatovici Territorial Defence, TO, because he was a policeman before the war. He was an active-duty policeman. They were looking for my son, Elvir Mujkic, and they were looking for Junuz Mujkic, too." And so on and so on. [Interpretation] Mr. Mujkic, who suggested to you that after five statements and amendments to the statements, and 12 years later -- you should involve Mirko Krajisnik in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, nobody suggested that to me. I did not mention that in my first statement because it was completely pointless. I didn't know what the reason for their visit was. However, when I came here to this Tribunal for the first time, I listened to the telephone conversations between Bakir Alispahic and Mirko Krajisnik. The second conversation was between Mirko and Momcilo Krajisnik. And then everything fell into place, the whole picture why they came to visit me. Alispahic said, Tell me his son was killed, tell me how much money you need, and this is where this conversation ends. Mirko wanted to see Dzino, the vojvoda, and Spahic [as interpreted] was to locate him, and that was the substance of this conversation. However, the conversation between Momcilo and Mirko Krajisnik, Mirko told Momcilo, I've just received a call by Bakir, but Spahic [as interpreted] is offering me money. We have Ramiz Mujkic in Rajlovac, who is seriously wounded. Then Momcilo responds by saying, If you don't have money, I can give it to you. He's looking for our snipers, What kind of money are you talking? So now I realised why they came to see me, and of course that was something that landed me in hospital. I don't know if there was another person --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slowly repeat the second part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, the interpreters were not able to catch up with your words, so could you repeat from the part referring to you didn't know if there was another person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never heard that there was any other fortunate man who had a fixator implanted in 1992 during the bloody conflict or the bloodiest conflicts that took place in the village of Ahatovici, and I can also mention Rakovica, the neighbouring village, as well as Svrake in Vogosca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, a fixator is implanted in patients who have broken bones. Why would it be implanted to someone else? Are you trying to say that we did not treat the wounded people?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I was in Blazuj Hospital. I knew that Serbian wounded people came and wanted to see me as some kind of freak. And I said that that's all I knew and that I couldn't confirm anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who suggested to you that in addition to Mirko Krajisnik, you mentioned the name of Mirko [as interpreted] Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you really think that I am mad, that I need someone to tell me what to speak about here? I can tell you at any time of the day what I went through and lived through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, the Defence has to examine why you -- and explore why you didn't mention this in your first, second, third, fourth and fifth statement, why you never mentioned such prominent figures before. How did it come about that suddenly you remembered Mirko Krajisnik, and later on Mirko [as interpreted] Poplasen? Did somebody tell you that Poplasen was the commissioner in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Vogosca is not miles away. I knew everything. But I'm telling you again there was no need for anyone to suggest anything to me. I used to see Nikola Poplasen on TV when I was at home. All these sessions and meetings that took place before the war, he was shoulder to shoulder with you, and he was among the highest echelons of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, when did you see Mr. Poplasen on TV?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992. So it was not just one day; it was every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was Nikola Poplasen's function at the time?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not a journalist or a reporter to be able to tell you which position he's held, because I simply don't know. I know that he was sitting next to you in some of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That were broadcast by TV?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, we had only Sarajevo TV. There were no other TV stations. In fact, there was TV Belgrade, but I was watching this on Sarajevo TV.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the transcript of your evidence in the Krajisnik case. That's 65 ter 22191. In the transcript, that's page 8005, and 84 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you stand by your statement that you knew Nikola Poplasen from television and from the political life?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only knew him from TV. I didn't know him personally, and that is the truth. And I made a declaration here that I was going to speak the truth, and that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at from line 3, the question is: [In English] "Do you know the name Nikola Poplasen?" [Interpretation] And then you say: [In English] "Not until that time, but the man was the president of the Serbian Republic and President Petric replaced him." [Interpretation] A new question: [In English] "Did you see Nikola Poplasen at any time in August 1992?" [No interpretation]: [In English] "I didn't see anybody, just the people who came to my cell." [Interpretation] So you hadn't seen Nikola Poplasen entering your cell with the other people. Now, I'm kindly asking you once again --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The translation was so unclear and so random that I cannot make any connection between the details. Can you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Just the people who came to my cell, so no."

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "So no," I think refers to Poplasen. Your Honours, this is taken out of the context. Where did I give this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked this question by this same Prosecutor, Mr. Gaynor, who questioning you now, and this is stated in the Momcilo Krajisnik case on transcript page 8005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, this is a transcript of your evidence given at the time of the trial against Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, so this is part of your evidence. I'll read it for you again. So the question was this: "Do you know the name Nikola Poplasen?" And your answer is: "Not until that time, but the man was the president of the Serbian Republic, and President Petric replaced him. "Q. Did you see Nikola Poplasen at any time in August 1992. "A. I didn't see anybody, just the people who came to my cell. So no." So that's the transcript of your evidence. So could you make any observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really surprised that this statement was recorded as such, because I couldn't have said this. It doesn't make sense, because I knew Nikola Poplasen from TV. I knew him. He came to my cell. However, the fact that she was the president of the Serbian Republic is something that refers to postwar period, so this is just a mish-mash of all various things. And, therefore, I cannot accept this as my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, would you like to see the video footage of your evidence on that day when you said what is recorded here?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is impossible for me to have said something like this. The essence is missing and the sequence is missing. I didn't see him -- there's mention of Petric. That was after the war, and I was not concerned about him at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who suggested to you to mention the name of Nikola Poplasen? The Prosecutor asked you if you knew him and whether he came to your cell, and you said he didn't. Now, who told you afterwards to mention Nikola Poplasen alongside Mirko Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I categorically state here that nobody suggested that to me. This was my experience that I, unfortunately, had. And I know these three men who came to see me. Nikola Poplasen and Mirko Krajisnik came, and this third man with a well-groomed beard who didn't ask me anything. You're asking me for the third time who suggested this to me, and that implies that I'm telling a lie, and that's not a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, do you know what Nikola Poplasen did before the war?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was a professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that before the war, Nikola Poplasen didn't play any role in the political life, nor was he a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't care about that. I didn't keep any record of who was a member or who was not. But I would really like to see if there were any Serbs who weren't members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, if I tell you that nowhere before the war, not in any meeting with me or in some other meetings, did he participate, what do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you that you are not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know which party was Nikola Poplasen a member of?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, is it possible for these questions not to be asked of me? I only mentioned that Nikola Poplasen came to visit me in my cell. What he did before the war is something that doesn't -- didn't interest me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you said that you saw him sitting next to me?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him on TV, but I don't know which position he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me help you, Mr. Mujkic. Nikola Poplasen was a distinguished professor at the Faculty of Political Sciences. He was not involved in any kind of politics, any kind of public life before the war. He was asked, as a person of a high reputation, to go to Vogosca to help the authorities there. Otherwise, he was president of the Serb Radical Party, and, as such, he won the election.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are not giving evidence. I think that question has been asked and answered. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, what I said, are you denying that? Are you denying that he was president of the Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I am not interested in that at all. I never mentioned the position he held before the war. I saw him with you, and I know that he was president of the municipality in Vogosca during the war. After the war, he was president of the Serbian Republic, and Wolfgang Petric, the high representative, removed him because of what you said, right, the wonderful reputation he enjoyed. And we all know full well what that was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let you see now how come you mentioned out of the blue something you refer to in the proofing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 226190, 65 ter, can we have a look at that. Can we have that transcript page from the Krajisnik trial -- can that be admitted, and all the previous ones, the ones we displayed previously?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you mean in their entirety?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not necessarily; just individual pages, the pages we displayed and that were commented upon by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from you, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No objection to that request, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I don't remember how long those statements were, but we'll admit the relevant pages. If it is short, there's no problem in admitting them all, but we admit what we have seen. Shall we give the numbers, respectively? First, the 92 bis statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The 92 bis statement, 65 ter 22188, will be Exhibit D1101. The 1998 statement, which is 1D3269, will be Exhibit D1102. The 2000 statement will be Exhibit D1103. That's 1D3268. And the transcript page, 22191, will be Exhibit D1104.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see how you remembered all of this all of a sudden just before you testified in Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have what I already mentioned, 22190.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is additional information that you provided to the OTP just before you testified. Let us see where it says -- the lower third of the page, the 10th line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it will be better for you to explain the nature of this document, what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You gave additional information to the OTP in relation to your statements and all of these things that happened after you were taken prisoner and after you were taken to the prison in Planjo's house. Now, I would be interested in the following: Do you remember that you provided, on the 1st of November, 2004, just before you testified in the Krajisnik case, that you provided some supplemental information?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot. I did not keep a diary as to when I said what. But if it has my signature there, I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are not directly quoted here. You are being interpreted here by the learned Mr. Gaynor. I'm going to read this out to you, and you are either going to recognise it or not: [In English] "During the witness's detention at Planjo's house, he witnessed a number of events of humiliation and cruelty carried out by 'weekend Chetniks' and prison guards, such as, first, forcing a May detainee to eat used cigarettes and to perform oral sex on another male detainee in the presence of guards and other detainees; and, second, forcing detainees to dive off the high fence onto concrete." [Interpretation] You provided a description here, and you seriously accused people, and this is appalling. However, you never mentioned any of that in your previous five statements given to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to the OTP, you never mentioned that. You remembered that when you were supposed to appear before this Court and testify against Momcilo Krajisnik; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. No one ever asked me about these things that happened. Quite simply, in my first statement -- I mean, I wish I could erase all of this from my memory, and I wish I had never seen any of this, but it is true. I was with an investigator. I think that he was from Australia. And we went to Planjo's house. I saw a photograph -- last Tuesday when I was being proofed here, I saw a photograph of Planjo's house, and also there was this picture of the bus, the massacre that occurred at Sastina [phoen], and he asked me what the attitude of the Serb guards was towards you then, you, the detainees. Then I spoke of this excessive conduct -- excuse me for a moment. The man was appalled by what I told him. I mean, when you get there and when you actually see the spot, and when you see that he jumped there to prove that he could swim. So those two statements were afterwards included in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So you were instigated by the Australian investigator?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, he did not instigate me. He just asked me what the attitude was. He didn't force me to say anything. I just told him about what had happened. You are twisting things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you say that in your first statement to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Well, to tell you the truth, I did not know at the time how far all of this would go, and nobody really asked me anything. They knew about torture. Sir, you know all of that full well, except that you are evading the truth. Not even the prison of God is good, let alone a Serb prison. I'm not saying that prisons are much better, I mean, other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Muslim prisons?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the prison of God is not good, nobody's prison is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us see what you said in your amalgamated statement, that is 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can we have this admitted as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. But when was it, Mr. Mujkic, that you said to the Australian investigator about the horrible incidents during your detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please don't take my word for the date, but before I came for the first time in 2004. We were there in the summer, and then I came in October/November 2004 for the first time, so I cannot say exactly what the date was, but it was summertime, it was very hot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted as Exhibit D1105.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, were you a member of the Crisis Staff in Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. I state that with full responsibility. However, upon orders of the Crisis Staff, I remained in Butile Barracks until the 9th of May. And then on the 9th of May, I escaped, because they wanted to put a uniform on me and to issue weapons to me, and then I could not go home. On the 9th of May, Sokolje was attacked, because that day was not really a normal day at the Butile Barracks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll go back to that. Let's look at 65 ter 22188, page 16, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is your statement to the AID in 1996, that is, the secret police of the Muslim part of Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave a statement at the police building. I mean, quite simply, I wasn't interested in who was who. As for the AID, I don't really know people. For the most part, they wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness. Other microphones are on. Could they all please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, it's page 18, and in Serbian, it's page 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure the interpreters followed the last bit of your question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Yes, I think everything was interpreted, but with great difficulty. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 16 in Serbian and page 18 in English of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you look at the Serbian page, look at the name of Alija Delimustafic in line 15. I think that is going to help you find that page, capital letters. And over here in English, it's around the middle: [In English] "To TO: I informed the commander of the TO, Hasan Mujkic ..." It says: "I informed the commander of the TO, Hasan Mujkic, about this, who told me that he was working on the order of Alija Delimustafic, the then minister of the interior, and he showed me a fax message that he had received, which said that the army barracks in Butile should not be attacked. Three or four days later, a message came from Delimustafic that the army barracks in Butile should be taken. It was already too late because we found out that, in the meantime, intervention units of the Serb volunteers, called the White Eagles, had arrived there." Let us see now how you explained all of this in your testimony in the Krajisnik case. It's the very same occurrence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, let us remember this page, and now let us have 65 ter 22191. 22191, page 150 in e-court, and 9240 in the transcript, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at line 14:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Q. Now, do you agree with me, Mr. Mujkic, that you don't say anything there about that order from Mr. Delimustafic that the army barracks in Butile should be taken over was just a rumour being put about by women?" [Interpretation] Your answer: [In English] "It doesn't say so here, but that's the truth, because I didn't see the second fax and the statement doesn't say that I saw it." [Interpretation] Question: [In English] "Now, you've gotten that last sentence there: 'It was already too late because we found out in the meantime.' Who was the 'we'?" [Interpretation] Answer: [In English] "Well, the Crisis Staff." [Interpretation] Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether I said it. It is possible that I did. I was not a member of the Crisis Staff. However, I just wish to explain here to clarify something. I haven't said that anywhere before, but I shouldn't go on forever. Six soldiers remained in Butile Barracks. They were ethnic Albanians. They did not manage to withdraw from the barracks. And there was a Croat who was left there, and I didn't know that he was a Croat otherwise I would have gotten him out, because I did get five Croat soldiers out, anyway. During the night, because he was my messenger, because I was a mechanic and the bakery in Butile had to operate, and then this messenger would come to see me whenever possible and he brought me news as to what was going on, and then he said, The barracks can be taken, because Nikola Soput's unit has left and there are only a few drunken reservists there. And I told Hasan Mujkic about that. He sent a fax to Delimustafic. The fax returned: "Do not touch the Butile Barracks. I saw that, and I guarantee that that's the way it was. Soon afterwards, three, four, five days later, whatever, Hasan called me and said, A fax arrived that the barracks should be taken. A soldier did not come to see me after that. And I said, I'm not going there anymore. And that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Crisis Staff of Ahatovici, did it place any roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not place any roadblocks, but we had three trenches opposite us, because Ahatovici and Dobrosevici are separated only by a road, and we are about 50 metres from the road. That's why we had three trenches where weapons were. People came there in shifts, the weapons stayed there, but we did not have any roadblocks, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it says here that you blocked the approaches to Ahatovici and Dobrosevici, right, and that was ordered by the Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true, because Dobrosevici was primarily populated by Serbs, so it was not possible for me to go in front of a Serb house and to put a roadblock there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us have a look at this now --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a number for this transcript page that we have shown just now, transcript page 9240, the Krajisnik transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to tender it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we add it to the already-existing transcript or shall we admit it separately?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll add it to the previous one, which is Exhibit D1104.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that you did not block the approaches to Ahatovici and Dobrosevici because Dobrosevici was populated by Serbs, predominantly by Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I wasn't in the Crisis Staff. There was nothing else I could do. As for the roadblocks, I don't know. My house is at the beginning of Ahatovici, and across from there immediately is the settlement of Dobrosevici. My neighbours across the street were Serbs. My house was on the right-hand side. There were no roadblocks there, other than two roadblocks the Reljevo and Bojnik bridges. These were two main arteries leading to the town. I mean, what would be the point of the roadblocks if you cannot go to town? Why would I be going to Dobrosevici?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On line 21 -- page 20, line 26 of today's transcript, you say: [In English] "So it was not possible for me to go in front of the Serb house and to put a roadblock there." [Interpretation] Let us now see what you said in your statement from 1996. This is the same 65 ter 22188, on page 15 and page 17 in the English. 65 ter 22188.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we tender this page 16 as well? We can add it to the same number, the page 16 where we talked about Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of the fact that the witness is putting quite -- that the accused is putting quite a number of pages from these statements to the witness, I submit that the easiest thing might be to do, to admit the statements in their entirety, both of the prior statements that have been shown to the witness by the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would need a lot more time, then, for the cross-examination, because then I would need to shed light for the other aspects. All I'm interested in is what I'm citing in the courtroom. If I get more time, then I have nothing against that, but let's not lose any more time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, let's do that. Given that we did not admit so many pages so far, so we'll follow that. That will be added to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 17 in the English so that everyone can see what we are looking at. In the Serbian, it should be page 17; page 3 in the actual statement. What I'm looking at here is page 5, actually. It should be page 3 in the Serbian, and in the English -- actually, that is page 15 in the e-court in the Serbian, page 15 in the e-court in Serbian. And English, page 17 in e-court. Thank you, and let's get the correct page in the English. Page 17 in the e-court, and that is actually page 4 in the statement, itself. The English is good and the Serbian is good. The last paragraph in English, and now we will see where that is in the Serbian. The bottom third in the English. It says: "Armed Serbs set up barricades on the road as early as March as an introduction into war activities, and they controlled the traffic and passengers with a constant mistreatment. As a reply to their activities, we also set up check-points in the villages of Ahatovici and Dobrosevici ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you state that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't have said anything like that, because I was not in the Crisis Staff. It's not just -- Ahatovici is not just the place where my house is, it's a broader area, and it doesn't make any sense for us to be setting up check-points in Dobrosevici. There were two main barricades on the two bridges, and whoever passed that way would experience mistreatment, and all entrances and exits were monitored.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this statement, though, you said that you did place a roadblock in front of Dobrosevici. Did somebody change or alter these statements, and do you stand by what you said there?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible to have that in Dobrosevici. It's Serbian all the way from Dobrosevici to Ahatovici, it's all Serb houses. Sir, I mean, as I said before, I cannot go in front of a Serbian house and place a barricade there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We're going to see later how that goes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 65 ter 90219, and can we add this page, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not already in the evidence, or only part of it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you let us know the page numbers of this document which we have already admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We admitted -- or asked to have page 16 in the Serbian and page 18 in the English, then here we have page 15 in the Serbian and page 17 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are admitting from 16 to 18, the pages. That being the case, I see no problem. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 65 ter 90219. This is your consolidated statement, paragraphs 35 to 38. That's in English, yes, the consolidated statement. 65 ter 90219, consolidated statement of Mr. Mujkic, paragraphs from 35 to 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now here you describe the events in Gornja Bioca. Do you remember describing that on this page of your statement?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 36, where it says: "Unfortunately ..." [In English] "... I did not meet up with our group. Instead, I encountered Serbs near the village of Gornja Bioca who had been taken over the village and were now pushing from the north. These were voices of the Serb soldiers going from Ilijas. According to the way they spoke and the swear words they used, I realised that it was the Serb Army." [Interpretation] So here you assert, before this Tribunal, in this statement that you were personally at that place, at that time, and that you concluded that it was the Serbian soldiers because they were swearing?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very familiar with the way Serbian soldiers speak. I was born there. I was 44, and I had lived there all that time, so I am very familiar with that jargon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer begins with: "Yes," for the purposes of the transcript. Please, can we note that the witness first said, "Yes," at the beginning of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The other soldiers don't swear; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can explain. For example, somebody would pronounce "bread" in a different way. For example, they wouldn't say "hleb," they would say, "leb," and this is something that I heard when I came to that place. And I could tell because they were dropping the Hs. The houses were empty, there was nobody there. Bioca was occupied the day before, so these forces started moving from Ahatovici forward towards the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break, if it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, if I may just round off this part, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not his amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it's P2314.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then look at 65 ter 22191, please, so that we can see what you stated in the Krajisnik trial. 65 ter 22191, page 25 in the e-court. And in the transcript, this is page 7946, line 10: [In English] "On the 22nd of August, I was brought from the hospital, Zica Blazuj, the Ilijas municipality, to Planjina Kuca, Planjina house in Semizovac. "Q. Now, sir, you said that the population of Gornja Bioca had been taken away to the school of Donja Bioca. Who took them away?" [Interpretation] Answer: [In English] "Sir, Your Honours, I can't say -- or rather, on the basis of their stories and what they said, this was done by the Serb Army, the Serbian soldiers, the units of the Ilijas municipality, in fact. I can't comment. I can't guarantee. I didn't see it myself. But what I did see ..." And so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So there is no mention of swear words or anything about you hearing and being able to recognise the rhetoric of the Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, you cannot take it like that. We're talking about some 20 days -- actually, three months after that. I heard the swear words on the 31st of May, 1992. I'm a little bit unsure about the dates here. As for the people in Semizovac in prison --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I can raise this in redirect, but if the accused is going to put that part of the answer to the witness, he should carry on a little further down through the answer and put the rest of it to the witness. I think he knows the part I'm talking about. Just simply the next three sentences, if he could put those to the witness, out of fairness to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's look at it: [In English] "What I did see and I did happen to meet those Serb soldiers who had already cleared Bioca and moved towards Ahatovici. So there was an order to this. I didn't see that actually happen, but judging by what they said, yes, because the 3rd unit wasn't there, the one that could have done that."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it's the whole answer and it's different from what you said in paragraph 36 of the consolidated statement; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mixed up a lot of things here. I understand your status and I understand that it's in your interests to mix things up, but you cannot mix things up because I am going to say everything in the sequence according to the dates as things happened. I lived through that. It's my life. Nobody wrote it down for me to be able to learn it off by heart.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I will really need to have some extra time. I'm really frustrated by this lack of time. I mean, we can take the break now, but I would really like to ask for an entire session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add this page to the Exhibit D1104. And we'll have a break for 25 minutes. We'll resume at seven minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. From the document 22188, 65 ter, can we have pages --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the page numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are pages, in e-court, 19 and 22, Serbian and English respectively, and the second part is number 10 and 11, Serbian and English respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say you are tendering those pages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, they will be added to the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, you were born in 1948; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you born in Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Ahatovici in Rajlovac municipality at the time or was it the district of Rajlovac which later became the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, we were part of Novo Sarajevo municipality. And when Novi Grad municipality was established, which is about 10 kilometres from Novo Sarajevo, we became part of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that up until 1958, when you were 10, Rajlovac used to be a municipality, and Ahatovici was part of that municipality?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. A 10-year-old child did not necessarily need to know in which municipality or district he lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I object on the ground of relevance. It's a totally irrelevant question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have document 1D03259. Your Excellency, I would like to remind you that Donia and other witnesses, including this witness, objected to the process of establishing the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac. Our proposition was that it used to be a municipality, that it was abolished and driven into poverty because all the major economic assets were moved to Novi Grad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is written in your birth certificate?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I was born in Ahatovici village and that I was a citizen of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No municipality?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Novi Grad municipality. It is true, there was a register office in Rajlovac, and these records were moved to Pale. I know that because I work at Novi Grad Municipality and I am familiar with these procedures. And even UNPROFOR had to intervene for those records to be returned to Novi Grad municipality that belonged to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Rajlovac municipality never existed. Now, look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, look at this document. Why do we not have English translation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't have time, Your Excellency. We were going to translate the whole interview, but I only wanted to ask Mr. Mujkic whether he knew that Rajlovac municipality had existed until 1958 in which there were Orao factory, a distribution centre, Sprint, Sarajevo Gas, and other important economic enterprises were located there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, Orao is located within the compound of the Rajlovac Barracks, and it was part of the military complex. Therefore, it was never part of the civilian structure. The distribution centre was built in the 1980s, and that used to be just an agricultural co-operative with barren fields. And there were about 50 houses there, the land taken from the farmers, pursuant to Tito's decree, and taken to -- and given to the co-operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can say whatever you like. This municipality was renewed in February 1992 as a municipality, which means before the war.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My dear sir, we had barricades at the time. The first barricades were set up in January on the Reljevo Bridge, and no Muslim could pass through. And there's only 300 metres from the bridge to the distribution centre, where your wartime municipality was. For your information, as the secretary of the local commune in 1996, I had an office in the distribution centre, because everything across the bridge had been demolished, and it was impossible to move because of the land-mines until a team established that there were no mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You deny that this was a municipality, and it says the contrary here.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was wartime. I couldn't go there, I never mentioned it, and I don't want to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that Orao company was not a civilian company?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orao was part of the military industry, and it was within the compound of the Rajlovac Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement of the 22nd, June 1997, page 2, you say that Orao was a civilian company, run by the military?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's one-and-the-same thing, it just being formulated differently. It was within the barracks, and no one had access there, other than through the main gate, and people were coming to and from work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we going to tender this interview into evidence and, actually, marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, when I asked you why we do not have an English translation of this document, you said you wanted to ask -- you wanted to ask the question to the witness, a question which is totally unrelated to this interview. You have been repeatedly warned by the Trial Chamber that you must have English translations of all your documents in order to use them in the courtroom. I think we have been very generous in permitting you to make use of untranslated documents thus far. And I also advise you to better organise your team and make use of the Tribunal's translation tracking system, et cetera. Please take this advice to heart. Next time, we may stop you using untranslated documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I fully understand and I accept that, but I have to say that this pace that I am trying to maintain is extremely difficult and neck-breaking. The question whether the municipality of Rajlovac was established for economic or political reasons was something that was raised by Prosecution witnesses, primarily Donia, and this was also mentioned by this witness, which I don't think they found too pleasant or acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But with respect to this clip, did the witness say anything about this one? I don't see any basis. Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President. I'm not in a position to comment on a very informed basis, because I have no idea what this article says, but I don't believe the witness has said anything to confirm this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, you worked as a civilian in the Yugoslav People's Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the 1st of October, 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a JNA employee, did you have certain obligations towards this army, in terms of loyalty, confidentiality, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, while it was the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when did you decide that it was no longer the Yugoslav People's Army and that you do not owe it any loyalty or any obligation to observe the Rules of Service?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Yugoslavia started to disintegrate, first it was called rump Yugoslavia, and the behaviour of the military personnel, officers and soldiers, was completely disrupted. When they removed the five-pointed star and put instead the insignia of the Serbian Army, that wasn't the Yugoslav People's Army for me any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that in September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that you like to refer to dates. However, I cannot confirm this. It was towards the end now of 1991, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you persuade, in September of 1991, your son to desert from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I managed to pull him out from Sremska Mitrovica during my third attempt to take him out. He was driving Seselj's men towards Vukovar and Vinkovci, and people used to ridicule him for the fact that they thought that he looked nice with a cockade. And in September 1991, I personally took him out of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in September 1991, the Serbs wore cockade -- the Yugoslav People's Army wore cockades?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is news to me, Mr. Mujkic.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you know that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you mention that earlier? Rather, you said that you persuaded him to secretly leave the JNA in September.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He served in Topci [phoen] there, in Belgrade, and he left in this 18-kilometre convoy. I didn't see it, personally. I saw it on TV only. And his unit was stationed in Sremska Mitrovica. Those were combat operations conducted against Croatia and Vukovar. And I don't know which person of a sound mind would allow his own child to go and fight for somebody else's interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that point, Bosnia was still part of Yugoslavia, and no decision was yet made to secede, nor was it recognised?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't on the Presidency of Bosnia. Therefore, I wouldn't like to remember these things. I wasn't part of that, and, therefore, I don't want to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this same statement from 1997, on page 3, you say the following, and that is while you were working at the barracks: "Because I was a Muslim, I try not to observe too many things, but at least on 10 occasions I saw people arriving in cars." Did you make a point of trying to observe as little as possible?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to an order of the Crisis Staff, I remained in the barracks until the 9th of May. And for your information, I wasn't on the payroll during the months of March and April, because we received our salaries in cash rather than through the savings bank. But I stayed behind precisely because I wanted to see what was going on. Butile Barracks was close by, and everything was normal until a military police unit with Colonel Nikola Soput came, and then everything went pear-shaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And pursuant to an order of the Crisis Staff, you stayed behind to spy on the army in which you were working as a civilian?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as soon as they removed their five-pointed star, they were no longer the army I worked for. They became a Serbian Army. And for your information, although you know that very well, the Croatian personnel, both the soldiers and the officers, left it. The people from Kosovo left it as well, as much as they could, because it was difficult for them to reach Kosovo. And Muslims were also leaving en masse. And as an electrician who was working at the bakery, Nikola Soput told me personally, Make sure that there is bread for each soldier, and for the rest, don't have any problems. And that is why I stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, a minute ago you said that you stayed as ordered by the Crisis Staff, and I think you repeated that in your 1996 statement, and that the purpose of that was to inform the TO of Ahatovici about the developments in the barracks. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's it, and I'm not ashamed of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the people of Ahatovici, in February 1992, which means before the elections and before barricades, introduced nightly patrols and that they had been preparing for war. They didn't have enough weapons, but you, nevertheless, had permanent positions and dugouts around the village?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have enumerated so many things. I don't remember saying anything to that effect, but it is true that we had three trenches facing Dobrosevici with three automatic rifles, and people rotated, because the remaining weapons were hunting rifles or some make-shift rifles made of water-pipes. You might not believe it. But as for these sheds and barricades that you mentioned, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this statement, which is 65 ter 22188 from 1997? It's page 3 in hard copy, and I don't know which page it is in e-court. So page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting: Mr. Mujkic, can we agree that the first barricades were erected on the 1st or 2nd of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which barricades are you having in mind, specifically? Because you are moving left and right, I would like you to tell me exactly which barricades you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first barricades erected by the Serbs. Were they erected on the 1st of March, after the killing of a member of the Serbian wedding party in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to talk about Sarajevo. I had no need to go to the city because my house was on the left bank of the River Bosna. I didn't go to the city in those days because it was risky. Therefore, I'm not going to answer this question. And as for these two barricades on the bridge, it is true that they were erected, and initially it was possible to pass through. But later on, public transportation buses would stop people, ID would be checked, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The checks were carried out in April, after the war broke out in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in March too, sir. And in February, the barricade on the bridge in Reljevo had already been placed because - how shall I put this? - there are 500 metres apart. It's only the Bosna River that divided them. Well, no Muslim could get through that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did no one ever report on this in the media or in official reports, that before the 1st of March, there were some barricades, Mr. Mujkic? How come nobody knows that there were no barricades?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you where I worked, and I worked there as an electrician. And I wasn't a journalist, I wasn't supposed to send reports to the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that this is that statement, 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Try page 8.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the 92 bis package, 22198, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I meant the B/C/S 8, the next page for the English. Is this it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please focus on this: "People in the village of Ahatovici ..." The fourth paragraph from the top: "People in the village of Ahatovici introduced, in February 1992, some neither patrols after the Serb reservists placed a check-point across the Bosna River right by the barracks." Were there any Serb reservists there in February 1992 or was this the JNA fully legitimately in Bosnia, and Bosnia was part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, soldiers who did their military service had an extension of three months, and then six months, because new soldiers were not being brought in. At the time, reservists came, and they were arming. Some of them stayed in barracks, but sniper shooters went outside the barracks. They were just issued with camouflage uniforms and sniper rifles, and they left the barracks. And I believe, and I say this with full responsibility, there were reservists at the end of February and the beginning of March at the Butile Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Vehbija Karic, Enver Hadzihasanovic, and Karavelic? I'm not sure about Karavelic, actually. Were they still in the Command of the 2nd Military District, the 4th Corps in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Karavelic, but I know about Enver Zejnilagic, because he was commander of the Butile Barracks. And for your information, I can say to you that I took his car out. He had a Skoda, a new Skoda car. It had only 2.000 miles on it. And he left the gate, and there was no -- there were no guards there. But before the Bosna River, I gave him his car and we said goodbye, and I never saw him again. I don't know about the others. I didn't go up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at this same paragraph. This is what you're saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next for the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, you say: "After April 1992, the Muslims were not allowed to pass at all."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The previous page, page 3, the page --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same in Serbian, the same paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "The village of Ahatovici ...." Do you see there: "At first, they did not check anyone. After, they started doing random checks. After April 1992, Muslims were not allowed to pass that way at all. Serbs, however, could pass check-points at any time. This check-point did not stop me from arriving at work, but only from arriving in Sarajevo." Do you know that after the 5th of April, front-lines were established in Sarajevo, and that's why you could not get into Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying now and I'll say it again: I had no need to go to Sarajevo because the barracks were only 2 kilometres away from my home on the left bank of the Bosna river, so I didn't have to go to that check-point. As for Sarajevo, when the front lines were established, you're supposed to know that because you're the one who organised them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're going to leave your remarks aside. Let us look at the next paragraph: "We patrolled only during the night." And look at this, what it says here: "There was no co-ordination with larger units." You had Territorial Defence, 200 men, and there was no co-ordination with larger units. The TO was not well armed, but they did have some permanent positions around the village, dug outs, and cottages. When did you build all of that for war purposes?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no dugouts there ever. I don't know how this came up. I do not remember saying that. Trenches, everyone knows what a trench is. And then a tarpaulin is placed on it so that rain would not fall into it. But - I don't know - say howitzers, mortars, et cetera, we didn't have that kind of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was it that you knew, Mr. Mujkic? What was it that you knew and that other people did not know, and how come you then sent your daughter to Germany in April 1992? Or did others also know and send other people out?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew because I watched you on TV every night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you sent your daughter to Germany, and your son stayed in the Territorial Defence; right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also begged him, besieged him, not to leave, and he said, Father, the Chetniks are going to come here, and you don't know what the Chetniks are. They put a cockade on my head. I know. So, psychologically, I'm at peace from that point of view. Regrettably, I still don't know where his bones are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anybody else send their children out, civilians?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC [Resumed]
